planting.note: Root stem cuttings and set out in spring once nights stay above 40F; grow in bright sun for the clearest leaf color.

directions: This collector cultivar forms an unusually deep, cup-like rosette of apple-green leaves on an upright stem, with the leaf margins blushing pink wherever light is strongest. Give it full sun and sharp drainage; a mineral-heavy succulent mix with occasional deep watering followed by a full dry-out keeps the stems from stretching and rotting. Named for the small Arizona art town rather than any botanical feature, it is a reminder that many Aeonium trade names come from where a grower first noticed and selected the plant rather than from its appearance.

planting.note: Propagate from stem cuttings in spring; bright light brings out the strongest pink flush.

directions: A heavily branching selection, this cultivar swirls lime-green centers into vivid bubblegum-pink leaf tips once it gets strong light. Let the succulent mix dry out fully between waterings and expect leaves to bruise easily in transit or rough handling, though they recover quickly with steady sun and a return to normal watering. Because it branches so freely, a single plant eventually forms a dense, multi-rosette mound rather than staying single-stemmed like many Aeonium cultivars.

common_name: Wheels of Fascination Aeonium (Spiral Pinwheel Aeonium)

planting.note: Start from rooted cuttings in spring; strongest spiral patterning and color develop in full sun.

directions: The leaves of this cultivar twist into a tight, visibly spiraling pinwheel rather than lying flat, giving the rosette a pleated, almost mechanical look that intensifies with age and sun exposure. Keep it in full sun with a very fast-draining mineral mix, watering only when the pot is bone dry, since Aeonium rosettes this tightly packed are prone to rot if moisture sits at the crown. It belongs to a small family of similarly playful-named selections from the same breeding program.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring; tolerates more handling than most Aeonium due to its thicker leaves.

directions: True to its name, this cultivar opens into a flat, open rosette of thick, rounded green leaves perched on a modest stem, coloring up orange to copper at the tips under bright light. Its leaves are noticeably stiffer and less prone to bruising than those of thinner-leaved aeoniums, making it a more forgiving choice for container growers who jostle their plants moving them in and out for winter. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage and let the pot dry completely between waterings, cutting back further during its natural summer rest.

common_name: God of Fire Aeonium (Burgundy-Bronze Rosette Aeonium)

planting.note: Propagate from cuttings in spring and give maximum sun; color depth fades noticeably in shade.

directions: Leaves on this upright cultivar shift through deep burgundy, bronze, and olive-green as light intensity changes through the season, living up to its dramatic trade name. It wants as much direct sun as you can give it, since the fiery pigmentation washes out to plain green in lower light, and a mineral-rich mix with a thorough dry-out between waterings keeps rot at bay. Like most showy Aeonium selections it reproduces far more reliably from cut, callused stem sections than from any other method, making a single plant easy to multiply over a few seasons.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring in bright but filtered light to protect the fine leaf margins from scorch.

directions: Unusually for the genus, this compact cultivar carries tiny white hairs along a finely serrated, pale-edged leaf margin, giving the whole rosette a delicate, almost frosted outline against its green center. Because true leaf-margin serration and trichomes are rare traits among Aeonium, it reads more like an Echeveria at a glance, which makes it a popular curiosity piece in mixed succulent bowls. Grow it in bright, filtered light rather than scorching full sun, keep the soil mineral-heavy and dry between waterings, and expect it to stay small and tidy enough for close-up container display.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring; red flushing deepens with stronger sun and cooler nights.

directions: This selection of the species Aeonium urbicum keeps the same tall, single-stemmed growth habit as the plain green form but washes the rosette with a deep pink-red flush whenever light is strong, fading back toward green in shadier spots. In mild, Mediterranean-type coastal climates it can build an unbranched stem to about two feet tall over several years before its rosette eventually flowers and declines, a typical life cycle for this group of tree aeoniums. Keep it dry-grown in gritty soil with full sun exposure, and propagate replacements from stem cuttings well before an old rosette finishes blooming.
